response: ## Finding `crime_00037` — **Oversized Raster** on `src/assets/hero-banner.png`, confidence 0.95. > byte size: 260,000 bytes (253.9 KB) > severity ladder: low ≥ 200 KB · medium ≥ 500 KB · high ≥ 1000 KB > format: png ## Verdict: request changes, don't block 253.9 KB sits at the **bottom rung** of the ladder — 27% over the 200 KB low threshold, less than half the medium threshold. Blocking a PR on a low-severity, `agent_risk` 0.14 finding with no correctness implication isn't proportionate. Two things push it above "nit," though: 1. **It's the landing-page hero** — almost certainly the LCP element. A quarter-megabyte on the critical path is a real Core Web Vitals cost, not a theoretical one, and it's paid by every first-time visitor on the highest-traffic page. 2. **The fix is `effort: quick`** — no build change, no code change, one re-export. There's no reason to merge it as-is and file a follow-up. So: request changes, re-encode before merge. If the PR is time-sensitive, merging with a same-week follow-up is defensible — this isn't a hard gate. One caveat on the evidence: the finding reports **bytes only, not pixel dimensions**. (Contrast `crime_00036`, which does report `32 × 32 px`.) So I can't tell you from the scan whether this is a 4000px export downscaled by CSS or an appropriately-sized but badly-encoded file. Check the intrinsic size before resizing — if it's already ~1600px wide, the win is entirely in the format change. ## Recommended transformation **Dimensions.** Don't ship one size. Ship a `srcset` ladder sized to the render area, capped at 2× DPR: ```html ``` For a full-bleed hero the top rung is **2560×~1280** (2× a 1280px max container, roughly 2:1). If the hero is constrained to a content column instead, drop the top rung to 1920w. Stop at 2× — 3× DPR assets are ~2.25× the bytes for a difference nobody can see on a phone. Set explicit `width`/`height` to avoid CLS, `fetchpriority="high"`, and **do not** lazy-load it. **Format: AVIF primary, WebP fallback.** AVIF is the right encode target here: - On photographic hero content it typically lands **20–50% smaller than WebP** at equivalent perceptual quality. - It handles **smooth gradients without banding** — the exact failure mode WebP's 8-bit YUV420 shows on sky/blur/duotone hero backgrounds, and the most likely reason this was exported as PNG in the first place. - Support is broad enough to be primary: Chrome 85+, Firefox 93+, Safari 16.4+ / iOS 16.4+. WebP stays as the `` fallback because it costs nothing at build time and covers older iOS and long-tail Android WebViews. Skip a PNG fallback entirely — every browser that can render this page supports at least WebP. Two things that would flip the recommendation to WebP-only: - **Text baked into the banner.** AVIF at aggressive quality smears fine high-contrast edges. (Baked-in hero text is its own bug — it breaks i18n and screen readers — so fix that instead.) - **CI encode time matters.** AVIF encoding is meaningfully slower than WebP. Rarely decisive for a handful of hero variants. **Budget.** Target **≤120 KB for the largest rung**, ~40 KB for the 1280w. AVIF at quality ~50–55 should clear that comfortably from a 253.9 KB PNG source. If it doesn't, the source is oversized and needs the resize too. **Worth asking in review:** why PNG? PNG for a hero means either (a) it's photographic and PNG is simply the wrong container — that alone explains the 253.9 KB, and format change gets most of the win, or (b) it's a flat graphic with few colors, in which case ask whether it should be **SVG or a CSS gradient** and disappear from the byte budget entirely. The `suggested_action` calls this out. ## Adjacent, not blocking The same PR area has two other asset findings worth a comment but not a gate: `crime_00032` (`partner-logo.svg` with two base64 rasters embedded — high severity, an SVG that isn't actually vector) and `crime_00036` (`check-icon.png` at 32×32 that should be SVG). If you're touching the asset pipeline anyway, an image optimization step in the build would retire all three and prevent the next one.
